clue.text: Little bit of dirt on garment taken to the cleaners

indicators.note: only a little bit of the word is wanted, namely its opening letter
in an across clue, one thing on another is written after it, so the first piece goes second

blocks.note: a fleece is a warm zip-up top
the first letter of dirt, placed after the garment

explanation.surface: A garment with a speck of dirt on it is sent off to be cleaned.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' puts the letter after the garment. 'Taken to the cleaners' looks like laundry but is slang for being swindled.
explanation.definitionFit: To be taken to the cleaners is an idiom for being cheated out of money, just as being fleeced is.

clue.text: European heard in the end

indicators.note: heard means we take the sound of the word, not its spelling

blocks.note: someone from Finland is Finnish, which sounds the same as a word with one N

explanation.surface: Someone from Europe gets a hearing at last.
explanation.definitionFit: A finish is the end or conclusion of a race or event, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Catch flipping associate? Not quite

indicators.note: not quite all of the word is used, so its final letter is dropped
flipping something over turns it the other way round, so the word reads backwards

blocks.note: a partner is an associate, as in business

explanation.surface: Trapping a partner who keeps changing sides is not quite managed.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the last letter of the associate, then read what is left backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrap someone is to catch them out by trickery, a verb synonym of catch.

clue.text: Foul cast — or cast keeping in the shade?

indicators.note: cast can mean thrown into shape anew, so the letters around it are reworked
keeping in means holding the jumbled letters inside the second word

blocks.note: taken as written, as part of the jumble
taken as written, as part of the jumble
the second cast, taken as written, wraps around the jumble

explanation.surface: A foul cast in a play, or a cast that stays out of the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'cast' is an indicator, the second a word that holds the others; the definition shares the word 'keeping' with the container device.
explanation.definitionFit: Colourfast fabric keeps its dye in the wash, so it holds on to its shade.

clue.text: Material used for some garden implements

indicators.note: only some of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A fabric that is used for making some tools for the garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Denim is the hard-wearing cotton twill used for jeans, so it is a material.

clue.text: Heavenly display from artist in London area

blocks.note: RA, Royal Academician, is the stock crossword artist
taken as written
Bow is a district in the East End of London

explanation.surface: A spectacular show staged by a painter in part of London.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow is an East London district, home of the Bow Bells that define a Cockney.
explanation.definitionFit: A rainbow is an arc of colours shown across the sky, so it is literally a display in the heavens.

clue.text: What town crier may do to jog memories?

blocks.note: first meaning: literally sound a handbell to call attention
second meaning: seem familiar and prompt recollection

explanation.walkthrough: A town crier was the official who walked the streets with a handbell making public announcements.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for something that sounds familiar and stirs a recollection is the same as the crier's literal act with a handbell.

clue.text: Taverns in Nova Scotia primarily

indicators.note: primarily asks for the first letter of each of the words before it

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letters of the province's two words

explanation.surface: Pubs found mainly in a Canadian province.
explanation.definitionFit: Inns are traditional pubs, so the word is a plain synonym for taverns.

clue.text: Somewhere in Oz small outlaw tucked into cheese

indicators.note: things tucked into something sit inside it

blocks.note: the soft French cheese
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
to outlaw something is to ban it

explanation.surface: A minor criminal in Australia hides inside a cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlaw' reads as a bandit, but it is a verb meaning forbid. Oz is informal for Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Brisbane is the capital of Queensland, a city in Australia, so it is a place in Oz.

clue.text: Traveller may be weary, struggling over a great distance

indicators.note: struggling letters are thrown into disorder and rearranged
in a down clue the jumbled letters lie over and around the distance word

blocks.note: the five letters rearranged
far means a long way off

explanation.surface: A traveller may be tired and labouring after covering a long way.
explanation.definitionFit: A wayfarer is someone journeying on foot, an old-fashioned word for a traveller.

clue.text: Neat trail, oddly enough, in part of South Africa

indicators.note: oddly points to the letters in odd positions, first, third, fifth and so on

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A tidy path, strangely enough, found in a South African region.
explanation.definitionFit: Natal was a province of South Africa, now part of KwaZulu-Natal, on the Indian Ocean coast.

clue.text: Nobody needs a single northern bird in New York

indicators.note: the other parts sit inside the abbreviation for the American city

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for New York
a single thing is one
N is the abbreviation for northern
a tit is a small garden bird

explanation.surface: Someone with nobody needs a lone bird from the north to settle in New York.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonentity is a person of no importance, which is what calling someone a nobody means.

clue.text: At sea a plump seal finds plentiful food

indicators.note: being at sea means being confused, so these letters are muddled up

blocks.note: all ten letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A fat seal out in the ocean finds plenty to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' fits the seal's home so well that it hides its job. Slap-up is informal British for lavish.
explanation.definitionFit: A slap-up meal is British slang for a large, lavish spread of food, so it is plentiful food.

clue.text: Musical foursome about the same

indicators.note: turned about, the word is still the same, so it reads identically in both directions

blocks.note: the Swedish pop group of two men and two women; the definition is also the word read both ways

explanation.surface: A band of four that sounds roughly alike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About the same' reads as 'roughly similar', but it means the name read backwards is unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swedish pop group of Waterloo fame had four members, so they were a musical quartet.

clue.text: Writing censored by editor taken to court

blocks.note: prose is ordinary written language
censored material has been cut
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A text cut down by an editor ends up in a legal case.
explanation.definitionFit: To be prosecuted is to have criminal proceedings brought against you, which means being taken to court.

clue.text: A bore rambling in the country shows restraint

indicators.note: something rambling wanders about aimlessly, so these letters are rearranged
the jumbled letters go inside the name of the country

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, rearranged
the country that holds the jumbled letters

explanation.surface: Someone holds back while a tedious person drones on in a foreign country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The country' needs a specific nation; France is the one that can wrap the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Forbearance is patient self-control, so showing it is exercising restraint; 'shows' plus the noun fits the clue's sense.

clue.text: After harvest fruit is seen again

indicators.note: after places one part next in line, following on from the other

blocks.note: to reap is to gather in a crop
pears are a common orchard fruit

explanation.surface: Once the crop is in, the fruit shows up again.
explanation.definitionFit: To reappear is to come into view once more, so the verb form means is seen again.

clue.text: Jerry's spaniel

definitions.note: the surname that completes the TV host's name

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of Jerry, the American talk-show host
second meaning: a breed of gun dog, English or Welsh

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one man's dog, but it splits into two: the famous Jerry's surname, and a breed of spaniel.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerry Springer hosted a notorious US talk show, and the springer is a breed of spaniel used for flushing game.

clue.text: Chaps covered with slippery tar on deck

indicators.note: something covered with another thing is wrapped inside it
slippery letters slide about and settle in a new order

blocks.note: the five letters rearranged
chaps are men

explanation.surface: Sailors smeared with greasy tar while out on the ship's deck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deck' looks like the ship's floor, but it is the verb meaning decorate; 'on' is part of the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: To ornament something is to adorn it, as decking the halls means decorating them.

clue.text: They won't keep beer I splash all over the place

indicators.note: scattered all over the place, these letters end up in a new order

blocks.note: all eleven letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A clumsy drinker sloshes beer everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They won't keep' sounds like a complaint about people breaking promises, but it describes food that goes off.
explanation.definitionFit: Perishables are foods such as milk and fish that spoil quickly, so they will not keep for long.

clue.text: Bother with false lashes

indicators.note: false here means not genuine, so the letters are faked into another order

blocks.note: the six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Putting on fake eyelashes is a nuisance.
explanation.definitionFit: Hassle is informal for trouble or irritation, so it is a synonym of bother as noun or verb.

clue.text: Extremely affluent females in capital

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two end letters

blocks.note: the first and last letters of affluent
hens are female birds, and slang for women

explanation.surface: Very wealthy women living in a big city.
explanation.definitionFit: Athens is the capital city of Greece.

clue.text: One vehicle for terrible ruler

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
a van is a goods vehicle

explanation.surface: A single car belongs to a dreadful leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' looks like a judgement, but it is the epithet of the first Tsar of Russia.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivan IV of Russia is known to history as Ivan the Terrible, so a 'terrible ruler' points to his first name.

clue.text: RAF accepts doubtful UFO?

indicators.note: doubtful letters are unsettled and can be put in a different order

blocks.note: all ten letters of the two words

explanation.surface: The Royal Air Force reluctantly admits there may be an unidentified flying object.
explanation.walkthrough: The RAF is Britain's air force, which suits the UFO story; the question mark flags the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A UFO is popularly imagined as an alien vehicle from another world, which would make it a kind of craft for travelling through space.

clue.text: Give the go-ahead for patent

blocks.note: first meaning: approve, authorise
second meaning: obvious, plain to see

explanation.walkthrough: 'Patent' suggests registering an invention, but here it is the adjective meaning evident.
explanation.definitionFit: To clear a plan is to authorise it, and something clear is obvious, just as a patent lie is.

clue.text: Clergyman is to lose his head soon

indicators.note: losing the head means the first letter is cut off

blocks.note: a canon is a member of a cathedral's clergy

explanation.surface: A priest faces beheading before long.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon is an old-fashioned word for shortly or in a little while, as in 'I'll see you anon'.

clue.text: Fruit grower's first to hire again

indicators.note: first asks for the opening letter only of the preceding word

blocks.note: the opening letter of grower
to re-engage someone is to take them on again

explanation.surface: A fruit farmer's priority is taking on the seasonal workers once more.
explanation.definitionFit: A greengage is a sweet green variety of plum, so it is a kind of fruit.

clue.text: Discrimination makes sense

blocks.note: first meaning: discernment in matters of style and beauty
second meaning: one of the five senses, the one using the tongue

explanation.surface: Prejudice is presented as perfectly reasonable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discrimination' suggests prejudice, but here it is the good kind: a fine eye for quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Taste is both refined judgement about what is good and the bodily faculty of perceiving flavour.

clue.text: TV executives think they are very important sailors

definitions.text: TV executives think they are very important

blocks.clueFragment: TV executives think they are very important
blocks.note: first meaning: audience figures, which broadcasters watch closely
second meaning: ordinary seamen in the Royal Navy, below officer rank

explanation.surface: Television bosses rate certain seamen highly.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Royal Navy a rating is a non-commissioned sailor, a usage common in British crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Viewing figures that rank programmes are called ratings, and the same word names naval ranks below officer.

clue.text: Put right about costume

blocks.note: re is Latin-derived for concerning or about
a dress is an outfit or costume

explanation.surface: Fixing something to do with an outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: To redress a wrong is to remedy or correct it, so it means to put the matter right.
